title: Cycle Budget Failure Modes & Slice Reconciliation Playbook
creator: Asha Menon
description: Problem: We observe repeated mid-cycle scope erosion when parallel workstreams hit resource contention or unexpected incidents. This ticket defines a documented playbook for identifying cycle budget failure modes, reconciling slice allocations across initiatives, and prescribing mitigations and automated signals to reduce ad-hoc scope cuts. Goals: 1) Catalog common failure patterns that drive unplanned scope removal; 2) Define quantitative thresholds and compensation rules for inter-team slice reconciliation; 3) Provide step-by-step remediations (e.g., temporary freeze, re-scope templates, role rotation triggers); 4) Deliver a light-weight simulator to run 'what-if' scenarios for the cycle planning meeting.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A failure-mode catalog with at least 6 empirically observed patterns (incidents, unplanned bugs, hiring delays, infra regressions, external integrations, stakeholder pivots) documented with likelihood and impact bands. 2) A reconciliation algorithm and decision table that returns a recommended scope action given two slices and a trigger (e.g., >20% burn rate delta or >3 missed milestones). 3) Playbook steps for PM leads and Eng leads with templates for temporary freezes, role reassignments, and communication notices. 4) A basic simulator spreadsheet and a stubbed web UI that can model 3 scenarios and export a recommended tranche-level action. 5) Sign-offs from Eng lead (Maya Chen) and Head of Product Ops (Ravi Patel).
notes: Context: Past cycles relied on manual ad-hoc negotiations that favored urgent customer-facing features; internal infrastructure and reliability work frequently lost allocation. We want a fair, repeatable process that preserves capacity for technical debt and reliability. This work will pair with the Cycle Capacity Dashboard prototype (GT-boards link) and the Capacity Estimator microservice. Considerations: keep overhead low for small teams, escalate only when thresholds breach, and make reconciling actions reversible (e.g., soft-freeze vs hard cancel).
